editorNote: Pictures are becoming commands: Sierra puts an icon-guided word processor on three rival home-computer families at once.
morningLine: HomeWord turns six writing chores into pictures while Atari sends its arcade catalog onto competitors' machines.

lead.headline: HomeWord Brings Icons to Three Computer Camps
lead.dek: Sierra On-Line gives Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari owners the same $49.95 picture-guided word processor.
body: A filing cabinet, a printed page, a printer, a disorderly page with an arrow, a question mark and a floppy disk now stand between the home writer and the command line. Sierra On-Line has introduced HomeWord for the Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari families, using six pictured icons to guide the program's principal jobs.

The screen can be divided into working text, a miniature preview of the finished page and a status chart showing memory and disk space. COMPUTE! reports optional joystick control, outlining, boldface and underlining, block moves, file merging, headers and footers among the features.

The cross-platform release is as important as the interface. Apple, Commodore and Atari owners cannot exchange programs freely, yet Sierra is treating them as one mass audience and giving each the same visual vocabulary. The approach echoes the mouse-and-icon excitement surrounding Apple's Macintosh without requiring a new $2,495 computer.

At $49.95, HomeWord places an unusually approachable writing system on machines already sitting in dens and bedrooms. Its icons do not abolish the keyboard, but they make a practical case that everyday software can explain itself with pictures rather than a memorized thicket of commands.

stories.headline: Atari's Games Defect to the Competition
body: Atari has released twelve familiar games for competing computers and consoles under the ATARISOFT label. Centipede, Defender, Dig Dug, Donkey Kong, Pac-Man, Robotron and Stargate head a list that reaches Apple II, IBM PC, Commodore, TI, ColecoVision and Intellivision buyers.

The move is a striking admission after the videogame shakeout: Atari's characters and arcade names may earn more when they travel beyond Atari hardware. Suggested prices run $34.95 for computer disks, $44.95 for computer cartridges and $40.95 for ColecoVision or Intellivision editions.

stories.headline: War Games Grow Up on the Commodore 64
body: Strategic Simulations is widening the C64 library with Battle for Normandy and Tigers in the Snow, two $39.95 historical simulations that ask players to command campaigns rather than merely chase a score. Both provide a solitaire option and period campaign detail.

Carrier Force goes further on Apple and Atari at $59.95, modeling four Pacific carrier battles with individual ships and aircraft, weather, visibility, time of day and imperfect sightings. Together the releases show serious computer war gaming moving across the same fragmented machine market as arcade conversions.

stories.headline: The $100 Home Computer Is No Longer a Fantasy
body: Mail-order advertising in April's computer press lists the VIC-20 at $79.95 and the Atari 600XL at $139.95, or $99.95 after rebate. A Commodore 64 appears at $189.95. These are dealer offers, not manufacturers' list prices, and availability may change.

The falling entry price extends to communications: a VIC 1600 modem is advertised at $59.95 and a Commodore 1650 at $109.95. A complete home-computing setup remains costlier once storage and display are included, but the first machine—and a doorway to bulletin boards—is rapidly becoming an impulse-scale purchase.

stories.headline: Color Graphics Become a $39.95 C64 Tool
body: Sophisticated Software's Grafix-Artist gives Commodore 64 owners a high-resolution color drawing package controlled by a special command language or joystick. The publisher proposes program screens, storyboards, design layouts and advertising displays.

Grafix-Artist lists for $39.95; a separate $29.95 Grafix-Printer utility transfers the high-resolution work to paper. The pair reflects a growing market for tools that turn an inexpensive home machine into a small creative workstation.

briefs.headline: Footloose Holds No. 1
briefs.text: Kenny Loggins' title song led the Billboard Hot 100 dated April 14 for a third week.

briefs.headline: Tommy Cooper Dies on Live Television
briefs.text: The British comedian and magician collapsed during a live television variety show on April 15 and died soon afterward.

worldAnchor.headline: India Occupies Siachen Glacier Positions
worldAnchor.summary: India launched Operation Meghdoot on April 13, airlifting troops onto key positions in the disputed Siachen Glacier region and beginning a high-altitude confrontation with Pakistan.
